Reviews · TVR Chimaera

Shaken, Not Rushed

The TVR Chimaera is a spy on holiday: dressed for dinner, packed for the Riviera and carrying a V8 it would rather not have to use. Spend a long weekend with one and you’ll understand why this is the TVR people fell for and kept.

By Douglas James · 14 minute read

4.1 sec
0–60 mph for the 5.0-liter Chimaera, by TVR’s handbook
2
Golf bags the trunk will swallow, by Autocar’s count
6,000+
Built, making it TVR’s best-selling car ever
1 dog
Credited with part of the design. You’ll hear about him at the bar

It’s still dark when the train rolls into Calais, and the first thing you notice in the gray light is the hood. It goes on for a long time. At the far end of it, 2 round headlights look out at France as if they’ve been here before. On the passenger seat is a map with a pencil line running all the way down to the Mediterranean. In the trunk is 1 bag for 2, plus a second pair of shoes, because you were promised there would be room, and there is. You turn the key. The V8 doesn’t bark. It clears its throat, the way someone does just before saying something you’re going to remember.

Every TVR has a personality. The Griffith is the hot rod roadster, all swagger and noise. The Chimaera is the one in the linen jacket. It knows which fork to use, it has packed properly for the weekend, and it would genuinely rather not make a scene. But it can. It most certainly can. That pairing of manners and menace in a single well-cut suit is why this became the TVR people didn’t just buy, but kept, cherished and drove to the far end of a continent.

Before any of that, though, there’s the cabin, and it deserves a moment. You sit low, looking down that long hood, wrapped in what PistonHeads once called “a couple of cows’ worth of leather.” The dashboard is wood, angled toward you and studded with round dials. It isn’t a race car’s cockpit and it isn’t a limousine’s lounge. It’s something in between that almost nobody else was making: a small room built for 2 people who intend to go a long way and enjoy every single mile of it.

Friday, 6:00 a.m.The Cover Story

The first few hours are all about the cover story, and the cover story is very good. TVR’s own press material in 1999 called the Chimaera “more of a grand tourer than any other model in the TVR range,” and on a wet French highway at dawn you understand exactly what it meant. The roof is up, the rain is beading on the paint, and inside it’s quiet and dry, which for a small British convertible designed in the early 1990s comes close to a miracle. The suspension, softened with Bilstein dampers and a rear anti-roll bar, lets the car breathe over broken pavement instead of skipping across it. The V8 settles into a low murmur in 5th gear. Your shoulders drop an inch.

Underneath, this is a close relative of the Griffith, with the same tubular steel chassis and fiberglass body, the same doors with no handles on the outside, the same total absence of ABS and traction control, and the same distinction of never having been sold new in America. The Long Way for Crackers tells that side of the family story.

What TVR changed was the tailoring. The tail grew, and almost all of the extra length went into a trunk that Autocar reckoned would take 2 golf bags. The ride softened. The whole car learned to settle at speed and let the miles slide by underneath. None of that made the Chimaera soft. It made it a car you could actually take somewhere, which is a different thing entirely, and a far more dangerous one, because now the V8 came along on every trip.

It made the Chimaera a car you could actually take somewhere, and now the V8 came along on every trip.

Friday, noonSomewhere South of Paris

By midday the rain has given up and the north is behind you. The autoroute unrolls south through farmland that seems to go on forever, and this is the stretch that grinds most sports cars, and their passengers, down to nothing. In the Chimaera it becomes the long, easy middle of the story. A 450 makes 285 hp, and out here you’re using a sliver of it, the engine barely awake, the hood pointed at the horizon. When a truck needs passing, a gentle squeeze does it without a downshift. Your passenger falls asleep somewhere near Dijon. That’s the highest compliment a grand tourer can be paid.

None of this is make-believe. Around 2003, Richard Hemsley bought a 1999 Chimaera 450 in Crystal Verde, a low-mileage car in close to perfect condition, and over roughly 4 years he covered about 30,000 miles in it, several of those trips to the South of France. Looking back in the TVR Car Club’s magazine 20 years later, he remembered how far it would go and how much it would carry, and he had no patience for TVR’s reputation for breaking down. His car, he wrote, “never once let me down.”

Then he did the most romantic thing a car owner can do. Years later, he went out and bought another one, a 2001 Chimaera 450 in Chameleon Blue.

That’s what sets the Chimaera apart from almost every other TVR. People didn’t just have a fling with it. They took it to meet their friends, they drove it to the far end of Europe, and when it was finally gone, some of them missed it badly enough to go looking for another. The Griffith made an errand feel like an adventure. The Chimaera makes an adventure feel like it was always the plan.

The Griffith made an errand feel like an adventure. The Chimaera makes an adventure feel like it was always the plan.

Friday, 7:30 p.m.The Forecourt

You drop the roof for the last hour, down onto the coast as the light turns gold. The sea is on one side, a low stone wall on the other, and the warm air smells of pine and salt. The hotel sits at the top of a gravel drive, and its forecourt looks like the cover of a magazine: a Ferrari, a Bentley, a Rolls-Royce that hasn’t moved since Tuesday. Beside them sits a Jaguar XK8 convertible in dark green, which is very nearly the car the doorman expected you to arrive in.

The Chimaera rolls in at walking pace, burbling, and the doorman looks twice. Not at the Ferrari. At you. He’s seen 100 Ferraris this summer. He has never seen one of these. Nobody on the steps can quite place it. It looks expensive in the way that never has to say so, with the long hood and round headlights of a better-mannered decade. You hand over the keys, and somewhere in the back of your mind a small, entirely private voice says: they have no idea what’s under that hood.

That’s the quiet pleasure of a Chimaera in a place like this. It doesn’t compete with the Ferrari, and it doesn’t try to. It simply belongs, which is harder.

The Jaguar is the neighbor worth studying, because the 2 cars are dressed from the same wardrobe. Both are British convertibles with a V8 up front, leather on the seats and wood across the dash. The XK8 went on sale in October 1996, the same year the Chimaera got its handsome new face, with a 4.0-liter V8 making 290 hp, within a whisker of the 450’s 285 hp. That’s where the resemblance ends. The Jaguar weighs 1,705 kg (3,759 lb), about 645 kg (1,422 lb) more than TVR claims for the Chimaera, and it’s 745 mm (29.3 in) longer. It takes 6.7 seconds to reach 60 mph. The Chimaera 450 needs 4.7.

Then there’s the bill. The XK8 convertible went on sale at £54,950 ($85,800), about £133,900 ($177,600) in 2026 money. In 1994, a Chimaera 400 cost £26,250 ($40,200), about £67,800 ($89,900) today. Roughly half the price, for the same idea, delivered with a great deal more urgency.

In The Long Way for Crackers, we measured the Griffith against a Mazda MX-5 Miata, because nothing showed more plainly how ridiculous that car was: the footprint of America’s favorite little roadster, with nearly double the power. The Chimaera is only about 100 mm (4 in) longer than a current Miata, and TVR claims it’s slightly lighter, so the joke still lands. But the Miata only tells half of this car’s story. The Miata is about lightness and honesty, a brilliant small roadster that has never once pretended to be anything grander. The Chimaera is a Miata-sized car that was dressed from the start to stand next to a Jaguar on a hotel forecourt without looking out of place. The footprint of a Miata, the wardrobe of a Jaguar, and a turn of speed neither of them could match.

Friday, 10:00 p.m.Every Spy Has a Scar

Later, in the bar, the man from the Jaguar asks about your car. Everybody does, eventually. This is when you tell him about the dog.

While the Chimaera was being styled, TVR boss Peter Wheeler’s German pointer, Ned, came bounding past the styling model and, in Wheeler’s own words, “took a bite out of the polystyrene model.” Most company bosses would have put the dog outside and called for the model makers. Wheeler looked at the bite, decided he liked it, and kept it. That chewed-out notch became the recess that houses the front turn signals, and it went into production. Every good spy has a scar with a story. The Chimaera’s has teeth marks.

It isn’t even the only TVR face shaped by damage. The Griffith got its look when an engineer cut into the foam model to see what would happen. At TVR, it seems, the best design work happened whenever somebody, or something, attacked the model.

The name fits better than anyone could have planned. The Chimera of Greek myth was a fire-breathing beast stitched together from a lion, a goat and a serpent. TVR’s version has the lion up front, a goat’s appetite for long mountain climbs and, if you lift off the throttle halfway through a wet corner, more than a little of the serpent at the back. A gentleman’s tourer named after a fire-breathing monster, with part of its face designed by a dog. The man from the Jaguar asks if you’re joking. You are not.

Like any good agent, it changed its look over the years. The early cars wore a mesh grille and, in the finest tradition of small British carmakers, tail lights borrowed from a Ford Fiesta, about as anonymous as a pair of shoes can get. In 1996 came a new nose that echoed the Cerbera coupe and a revised tail, and in 2001 the headlights went behind clear covers. The 1996 face is the one most people picture, and it’s a big part of why the Chimaera has aged so gracefully. Where the Griffith looks like a sports car having the time of its life, a late Chimaera looks like something very well-dressed that has been kept beautifully for 30 years. Often, it has.

Saturday, 6:30 a.m.The Gun in the Glovebox

Saturday starts early, before the coast road fills with tour buses. Your passenger is still asleep. You leave a note, take the keys and head up into the hills behind the coast, on a road that folds back on itself every few hundred yards with nothing but rock on one side and air on the other. For the first time all weekend, the spy is asked to step outside.

Every Chimaera carried a version of the same aluminum V8, and TVR offered it in 5 strengths over the car’s life. Hagerty describes the engine moving from a lazy burble at low revs to a “cultured roar” when you use it, and on an empty mountain road at dawn, you use it. 2nd gear, 3rd, the exhaust bouncing back off the rock wall, the long hood swinging into each hairpin and the tail squatting as you power out of it. It isn’t frantic. It’s a deep, rising thunder that seems to come from everywhere at once, and a few hairpins in you realize you’re laughing out loud, alone in the car, at nothing at all.

The one to fear is the 500. TVR’s handbook credits its 5.0-liter engine with 340 hp, 0–60 mph in 4.1 seconds, 0–100 mph in 10.2 and 167 mph flat out, and only about 600 were built. The 450 is the gentleman’s choice: 285 hp, 0–60 mph in 4.7 seconds and 160 mph, with enough torque to pull out of a hairpin a gear too high and not mind in the slightest.

Nothing stands between you and the consequences, either. The long throttle travel helps you meter the power, which is a polite way of saying the car trusts you to be sensible. In the dry, it flows from one bend to the next. When the road is still damp from the night, the serpent stirs, and you remember exactly why the myth gave the beast that tail. Power steering arrived as an option in 1995, which made town driving easier and, by most accounts, took a little feel out of a road like this one. Even on holiday, the spy expects you to pay attention.

By 8, you’re back at the hotel. Your passenger is awake, reading on the terrace, and asks where you’ve been. “Nowhere,” you say. The car, ticking quietly as it cools on the gravel, says otherwise.

Saturday, 1:00 p.m.The One People Married

Lunch is in a village square further along the coast, the roof down, the engine pinging softly as it cools beside a fountain. An old man in a flat cap walks a slow circle around the car, says something in French you don’t catch but completely understand, and goes back to his coffee. That’s worth more than any road test.

It’s also the Chimaera’s real achievement. The Griffith made TVR famous. The Chimaera is the one people took home and lived with. It became TVR’s best-selling car of all time, with about 6,000 built between 1992 and 2003 by TVR’s count, and more than 6,000 by Hagerty’s. The last one left the Blackpool line in 2003.

Those sales did more than pay the bills. It’s hard to imagine a company of TVR’s size finding the nerve to design its own engine for the Cerbera without the Chimaera selling steadily in the showroom behind it. The Griffith was the fling that got everybody talking. The Chimaera was the marriage that kept the lights on.

And people loved it the way you love something that’s always ready when you are. Not because it was perfect. It was a hand-built British V8 roadster from the 1990s, and it had its moods. They loved it because a long drive in it never felt like a chore, and a short one never felt ordinary. Because it could carry a weekend and still frighten a Porsche. Because it could cross a country on Friday and still make Saturday morning feel like an escape.

If the Chimaera is the spy on holiday, its sibling is the one who came home with a family. The Cerbera took this same idea, closed the roof, found room for 2 small rear seats and gave TVR its own engine. That’s a story for another day.

If you want one

Start underneath. The steel chassis is shared with the Griffith and needs the same specialist inspection before anything else: the outriggers, the central spine and the suspension mounts.

Listen to the engine. Look for oil leaks at the timing cover and listen for rattles that can point to piston slap, most common on the 5.0. A failed head gasket or a slipped cylinder liner can pressurize the cooling system. Hagerty put replacement top-hat liners at around £1,000 ($1,240) fitted in 2022, about £1,150 ($1,530) in 2026 money.

Know the changes. The Borg-Warner T5 gearbox that replaced the Rover unit in the mid-1990s is the tougher of the 2. Test every electrical item, check the windshield edges for clouding and the carpets for damp from a leaking roof.

Check the wardrobe. Half-hide trim was standard; full leather, heated seats and air conditioning were options. A car with the full set is the grand tourer TVR had in mind.

What they cost. Hagerty’s 2022 guide put a good 400 HC or 450 near £15,000 ($18,600), about £17,300 ($22,900) in 2026, and a mint 500 near £22,000 ($27,300), about £25,400 ($33,600) today. Most Chimaeras can already come to America under the 25-year rule, the very last of them during 2028, and The Long Road Home walks through the paperwork.

Sunday, 7:00 p.m.Shaken, Not Rushed

Sunday evening, and the last stretch of coast road before the long run home. The sea has turned the color of the car, the village lights are coming on below, and the V8 is idling along in a tall gear, ticking over like it has nowhere better to be. You know what it can do. You found out yesterday morning, up in the hills, with nobody watching. Now it’s back to being charming, and so are you.

That’s the whole trick of the Chimaera. It never pretends to be harmless, and it never insists on proving otherwise. It carries both sides of itself everywhere it goes: the linen jacket and the loaded glovebox, the bag in the trunk and the 4.1 seconds to 60 mph. Tomorrow night you’ll be home. You’ll park it, walk to the door, and turn around for one more look. You’ll be doing that for years.

The best spies never rush. They don’t have to. Shaken, not rushed, just as it should be.
